source.title: Negative Results for SAEs On Downstream Tasks and Deprioritising SAE Research (GDM Mech Interp Team Progress Update #2)

record.file_problem: Whole post text is present. Some referenced figures are represented only by descriptions, and a few links are marked TODO; the underlying figure values are not transcribed.
record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE-feature probing to a downstream task in Gemma-v2 9B IT and reports results bearing on whether sparse dictionary features can recover task-relevant information in an LLM. It does not test superposition geometry directly.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful-intent probe performance using SAE latents and SAE reconstructions, including comparisons with residual-stream linear probes. It does not measure feature overlap, near-orthogonality, feature sparsity or importance, overcomplete feature count, neuron polysemanticity, or feature dimensionality. Some results are described from plots without numerical values. Reported results from other papers and the post’s comments are not treated as study results.
record.test_reason: Probes on SAE latents and SAE reconstructions in Gemma-2 9B IT bear on whether dictionary features recover a model concept (V4). They also bear on whether SAE features are complete, canonical units (V5). Reconstructions lose OOD-relevant information, and which latents capture the concept depends on the SAE's training data. The authors argue current SAEs do not find the needed concepts. No superposition geometry, neuron polysemanticity or feature dimensionality is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude current SAEs do not find the 'concepts' needed for this task while a linear probe finds a useful direction. They leave open whether harmful intent is not a model concept or the SAE fails to learn it. They are now unsure whether even an optimal SAE should beat probes OOD, and they deprioritise SAE research.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE latent and reconstruction probes for harmful-intent classification in Gemma-v2 9B IT; it does not reproduce toy-model feature competition or measure superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer 20 was the most reliable tested location. Max aggregation was generally best, though fixed position -5 was comparable. Chat-data training improved probes relative to the original GemmaScope SAEs; tested finetuning variations showed no systematic probing difference.

fits_no_version.finding: JumpReLU and TopK SAEs develop high-frequency latents (>10% firing) that often seem uninterpretable. A quadratic-frequency penalty removes them at a small reconstruction cost.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The SAE training objective shapes which dictionary latents appear, including dense uninterpretable ones.

fits_no_version.finding: Frequency-weighted autointerp scores fall with latent frequency, and the ordering of SAE architectures differs from uniform weighting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The measured interpretability of dictionary features depends on how latents are weighted.

record.problems: The results concern one model family and one harmful-intent task. Many SAE-probe comparisons are described qualitatively from plots without numerical curve values or reported error bars. The authors note that their setup may be noisy and that their findings do not support confident extrapolation to all OOD settings.
record.rows_left_out: No reported probing result bearing on V4 was intentionally left out. Numerical values for SAE probe curves are not transcribed in the post text, so the relevant plot results are recorded qualitatively.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All of it: no capacity or importance analysis and no neuron polysemanticity.
Whether features are spread across many neurons. Only one model and one concept (harmful intent) are tested.
Stability across seeds or widths, and canonicity, are not measured directly. Completeness is probed only through one concept's reconstruction.

missing.what: Chat-data SAEs close 'about half the gap' to dense linear probes; this is the only quantitative summary of the SAE-probe gap.
In k-sparse probes, finetuned SAEs beat original GemmaScope SAEs, particularly at low L0. Mean-difference and L1 latent selection give similar results.
missing.locator: Using SAEs for OOD Probing, Results (k-sparse)

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4-only linkage misses that the reconstruction rows bear most directly on V5 completeness. Dense-probe rows are baselines and should not be linked. The evidence is indirect: a commenter (Marks) disputes that sparse-probe results test SAE completeness or crispness. All results come from one model, one layer and one concept, with no error bars.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity can arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Tests task-specific recovery of harmful-intent information using SAE probes in Gemma-v2 9B IT; does not measure how features are distributed across neurons or test other models and tasks.
Does not directly test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units. Probe and reconstruction performance on one task cannot establish those properties.
Does not measure whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
